blocks.content: Sometimes building an object from scratch is the expensive part, not using it.

Imagine an object that is only fully "ready" after a slow database call, a heavy computation, or several configuration steps. If you need ten more objects that look almost exactly like it, running that expensive setup ten more times is wasteful.
The Prototype Pattern offers a different route: keep one fully configured object around, and produce new objects by copying it instead of constructing it again.

This chapter walks through why cloning beats constructing in certain situations, how a clone method is implemented, and the single most important trap in this pattern, the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy.
Prototype is a creational pattern that creates new objects by copying an existing, fully initialized instance, instead of building a fresh one from raw inputs.
1. What Problem Does Prototype Solve
Object creation is not always cheap. A constructor might look innocent, but the work behind it can be anything but.
https://MyDSA-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499368809-763256332.png
blocks.alt: Flow comparing an expensive from scratch construction with a cheap clone of an existing prototype

blocks.content: ["Expensive setup, the object is populated from a slow database query or a network call.","Heavy computation, the object is the result of parsing, indexing, or running an algorithm before it is usable.","Complex configuration, the object needs many fields set correctly, and getting a fresh one right every time invites mistakes.","Runtime variation, the exact type of object to create is only known at runtime, and you have an example instance rather than a class name to instantiate."]
items: Expensive setup, the object is populated from a slow database query or a network call.
Heavy computation, the object is the result of parsing, indexing, or running an algorithm before it is usable.
Complex configuration, the object needs many fields set correctly, and getting a fresh one right every time invites mistakes.
Runtime variation, the exact type of object to create is only known at runtime, and you have an example instance rather than a class name to instantiate.

blocks.content: In each of these cases, once you have one good instance, making a copy of it is far cheaper than repeating the original construction work.

blocks.title: Not just about speed
blocks.content: Prototype also helps when construction logic is scattered or fragile. Cloning a known good object sidesteps re-running that logic entirely, which reduces the chance of building a broken object.
This is the core motivation. Instead of asking "how do I build this object," Prototype asks "do I already have one I can copy."
A quick real world analogy
Think of a bakery that keeps one perfectly risen batch of dough as a starter. Every new loaf is shaped from a piece of that starter rather than being fermented from raw flour and yeast each time.
The starter took time and care to get right. Copying from it is fast, and every loaf begins from a known good state instead of an uncertain fresh batch.
2. The Core Idea, Clone Instead of Construct
blocks.text: 2. The Core Idea, Clone Instead of Construct

blocks.content: At its heart, Prototype introduces a single new responsibility on the object itself, the ability to copy its own state into a brand new instance.
Every object that supports this exposes a method, usually called clone, that returns a new object of the same type with the same field values.
The two participants

["Prototype, the fully configured object you already have, acting as the template for future copies.","Client, the code that calls clone on the prototype whenever it needs a new object, rather than calling a constructor directly."]
items: Prototype, the fully configured object you already have, acting as the template for future copies.
Client, the code that calls clone on the prototype whenever it needs a new object, rather than calling a constructor directly.

blocks.title: A document template
blocks.text: Think of a report template that already has a header, footer, styling, and default sections filled in. Generating a new report is far quicker by cloning the template and only changing the content, compared to rebuilding the entire layout from nothing each time.

blocks.content: The client never needs to know the internal steps that produced the prototype in the first place. It only needs to know that calling clone gives back something equally ready to use.
This is a meaningful shift in responsibility. Creation logic moves off the client and onto the object itself, which is the part of the code that best understands its own state.
3. The Clone Method
A clone method is, at minimum, a function that builds a new object and copies every field from the current instance into it.
https://MyDSA-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499372141-554061162.png
blocks.alt: Sequence of steps inside a clone method from client call to an unchanged original prototype

blocks.content: Step 1, define a common clone contract
blocks.text: Step 1, define a common clone contract

blocks.content: Classes that want to support cloning usually implement a shared interface with a single clone method, so client code can clone any prototype without knowing its concrete type.
Step 2, copy the fields
Inside clone, a new instance is created and each field from the current object is assigned to it.
Step 3, return the new instance
The method hands back the freshly built copy, leaving the original prototype completely untouched.
This version works cleanly because every field is a simple value, a string. Copying a string never causes two objects to share mutable state.
The moment a field becomes an object or a collection, this simple approach quietly stops being safe.
That is the exact boundary the next section covers, and it is the part of Prototype that actually requires careful thought.
4. Shallow Copy versus Deep Copy
This is the single detail that makes or breaks a Prototype implementation.

A shallow copy creates a new object, but for any field that is itself an object or a collection, it copies the reference, not the underlying data. The original and the copy end up pointing at the exact same nested object.
A deep copy goes further, it creates new, independent copies of every nested object and collection too, so nothing is shared between the original and the clone.

{"headers":["Aspect","Shallow Copy","Deep Copy"],"rows":[["Top level fields","Copied into the new object","Copied into the new object"],["Nested objects","Reference is copied, same object shared","A new, independent object is created"],["Mutation safety","Changing a nested field affects both copies","Changing a nested field affects only one copy"],["Cost","Cheap, fast","More work, proportional to how deeply nested the object is"],["Typical bugs","Silent data corruption across supposedly separate objects","None from sharing, but must be implemented carefully"]]}
When every field is a primitive, shallow and deep copies behave identically. The difference only shows up once a field is a nested object, an array, or a map.

blocks.title: Why this matters so much
blocks.content: A clone is supposed to be independent. If two "separate" objects secretly share a nested list or object, changing one through what looks like its own private state ends up changing the other. That is one of the hardest classes of bug to trace, because the two objects look unrelated in the code.
Why the difference matters so much
blocks.text: Why the difference matters so much

blocks.content: The whole point of cloning is to get an independent object. If a shallow copy silently keeps a shared nested reference, the clone is independent in name only, and every mutation risks leaking across objects that look completely unrelated in the code.
5. The Bug, a Shallow Copy Sharing a Nested Reference
blocks.text: 5. The Bug, a Shallow Copy Sharing a Nested Reference

blocks.content: Consider a prototype that carries a list of default sections, an object nested inside it.
A naive clone method copies the reference to that list rather than the list itself. Both objects then look at the same underlying array.
https://MyDSA-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499374545-84589285.png
blocks.alt: Diagram showing a shallow copy sharing the same nested array so a mutation is visible in both objects

blocks.content: Nothing in this code looks wrong at a glance. The bug only appears once someone mutates the copy and notices the original changed too.
This is exactly the failure mode a deep copy is designed to prevent.
6. Implementing a Correct Deep Clone
Fixing the bug means the clone method must build a new nested object or collection instead of reusing the existing one.
https://MyDSA-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499376557-249957997.png
blocks.alt: Diagram showing a deep clone with its own independent nested array so a mutation stays isolated

blocks.content: Step 1, identify every nested field
Any field that is an object, array, map, or set is a candidate that needs its own copy, not a shared reference.
Step 2, copy each nested field independently
blocks.text: Step 2, copy each nested field independently

blocks.content: For arrays and simple collections, building a new collection and copying elements across is usually enough. For nested objects, calling their own clone method keeps the deep copy consistent all the way down.
Step 3, verify independence
After cloning, mutating the copy should never be visible on the original, and vice versa. That check is the real test of a correct deep clone.
The fix is small in every language, but it depends entirely on recognizing which fields are nested objects in the first place.

blocks.title: Deep copy is not automatically recursive
blocks.content: Languages that offer a generic deep copy utility still need every nested object along the way to support being copied correctly. A deep copy is only as deep as the weakest link in the chain of nested objects.

It is worth writing a small test whenever a clone method is added, mutate the copy right after cloning, then check the original was left untouched. That single check catches most shallow copy mistakes immediately.
7. A Worked Example, Cloning a Configured Document Template
blocks.text: 7. A Worked Example, Cloning a Configured Document Template

blocks.content: Picture a document template built once at startup. It is populated from a database call that reads default styling, a list of sections, and metadata. That call is slow, and it is wasteful to repeat for every new document.
Instead, the application creates the template once, keeps it in memory as a prototype, and every new document is produced by cloning it.
https://MyDSA-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783494361117-760968264.png
blocks.alt: Diagram contrasting a deep clone that produces an independent instance with a shallow copy that leaves a shared nested reference

blocks.content: On the left, cloning walks into the nested object and produces its own independent copy, so the new instance and the original never interfere with each other.

On the right, the shallow copy skips that step. Both instances end up pointing at the same nested object, so a change through one is visible through the other, an unpleasant surprise for whoever wrote the code expecting two separate documents.

blocks.title: Bulk document generation
blocks.text: A reporting service needs to generate five hundred documents that share the same base template but differ in a handful of fields. Cloning the prototype five hundred times, and correctly deep copying its nested sections and metadata each time, is far cheaper and safer than re-running the original database backed construction five hundred times.

blocks.content: This pattern shows up constantly in editors, games, and configuration heavy systems, anywhere a fully set up object is common and a mostly identical copy is needed repeatedly.
What actually happens during the clone
blocks.text: What actually happens during the clone

blocks.content: The template object receives a clone call. It builds a new instance, copies its simple fields directly, and for the nested sections list and metadata object, it builds fresh copies rather than reusing the existing ones.
The caller then only touches the handful of fields that make this particular document different, the title or a date, while everything else arrives already correctly set up.
8. Prototype versus Constructor and Factory
It is worth being clear about when Prototype actually earns its place over the more familiar alternatives.
https://MyDSA-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499378245-916134805.png
blocks.alt: Comparison of constructor factory and prototype approaches to producing a new object

blocks.content: Using a constructor directly

A constructor rebuilds an object from raw inputs every single time. That is fine when construction is cheap, but wasteful when it involves a slow call or heavy computation that a clone could skip entirely.
Using a factory

A factory decides which class to instantiate and builds a fresh object accordingly. It solves a different problem, choosing the right type, rather than avoiding repeated expensive construction. Prototype and Factory are not competitors, they can even be combined, a factory that returns clones of pre-built prototypes.
A useful way to tell them apart, a factory answers the question of which type to build, while Prototype answers the question of how to avoid rebuilding something you already have.

["Constructor, always builds from scratch, simplest option when creation is cheap.","Factory, centralizes the decision of which type to create, still builds fresh objects.","Prototype, skips construction entirely by copying an existing, ready to use instance."]
items: Constructor, always builds from scratch, simplest option when creation is cheap.
Factory, centralizes the decision of which type to create, still builds fresh objects.
Prototype, skips construction entirely by copying an existing, ready to use instance.

9. When Prototype Is Worth Reaching For
blocks.text: 9. When Prototype Is Worth Reaching For

blocks.content: Prototype earns its keep when you already have a well configured object and construction is the expensive or fragile part of the process.

If a new object needs a slow database read, a heavy computation, or many careful configuration steps before it is usable, and you frequently need near identical copies of it, cloning a prototype is almost always cheaper and safer than repeating that setup.

The one condition that cannot be skipped is getting deep copy right. A clone that quietly shares a nested object with its original is not really independent, and the bugs that follow are subtle and hard to trace.

If your objects are simple, made only of primitives, and cheap to construct, a plain constructor is usually the better choice. Prototype is a tool for the moments when copying a known good object is genuinely cheaper than building a new one.

["Construction is slow, expensive, or involves a database call or heavy computation.","Many near identical objects are needed from one well configured starting point.","The exact type to create is only known at runtime, as an example instance."]
items: Construction is slow, expensive, or involves a database call or heavy computation.
Many near identical objects are needed from one well configured starting point.
The exact type to create is only known at runtime, as an example instance.

blocks.content: Reach for it in those situations, get the deep copy right, and Prototype quietly removes a surprising amount of repeated, wasteful construction work.
